claims.text: Conventionally produced phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys generally exhibit marginal glass formation.
Conventionally produced phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys have limited amorphous-state thermal stability.
Ultra-rapid quenching will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys relative to conventional quenching.
Ultra-rapid quenching will improve the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state relative to conventional quenching.
High wheel speed and thin ribbon geometry in melt spinning can produce the proposed ultra-rapid quenching condition.
The comparison should hold composition constant and vary cooling rate.
Ultra-rapid quenching creates a more homogeneous, deeply undercooled liquid state.
A homogeneous, deeply undercooled liquid suppresses nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during solidification.
Increasing the cooling rate reduces atomic diffusion during solidification.
Increasing the cooling rate reduces crystal-nucleation kinetics.
Reduced diffusion and nucleation prevent crystallite formation.
Suppressing crystallite formation during quenching stabilizes the amorphous phase during subsequent thermal treatments.
Ultra-rapid quenching will produce a measurable increase in the critical cooling rate for amorphization.
Ultra-rapid quenching will significantly delay crystallization onset during thermal analysis.
The intervention will work only above a sufficiently high, but unspecified, quenching-rate threshold.
Substantial composition changes may eliminate the predicted benefit of ultra-rapid quenching.
Relative to conventional quenching, ultra-rapid quenching should yield a more homogeneous amorphous structure.
Failure to observe the specified differences in critical cooling rate, crystallization onset, and amorphous homogeneity would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes improved glass-forming ability, but the predicted and required result is a higher critical cooling rate. A higher minimum cooling rate makes amorphization more demanding rather than demonstrating the stated improvement; improved glass-forming ability would ordinarily correspond to a lower critical cooling rate or amorphization at slower cooling.
